triage.name: Reflux in Infants
triage.reason: Very common infant presentation of spitting up and irritability, diagnosed clinically with attention to warning signs.

rule_errors: patient.age.possible_max: over 2 for a newborn or infant condition; ages are in years
review_issues: auto-repaired: workup: 'Upper GI series (barium swallow)' was in initial, not_indicated; kept initial as a conditional order (only if Projectile or bilious vomiting, poor weight gain, or suspected anatomic obstruction)
auto-repaired: workup: 'Ultrasound of the abdomen (pylorus)' was in initial, not_indicated; kept initial as a conditional order (only if Projectile vomiting or suspected pyloric stenosis)

auto-repaired: workup: 'Esophageal pH/impedance monitoring' was in confirmatory, not_indicated; kept confirmatory as a conditional order (only if Diagnosis uncertain after clinical evaluation and trial of feeding modifications, or suspected refractory GERD)

auto-repaired: workup: 'Upper endoscopy with biopsy' was in confirmatory, not_indicated; kept confirmatory as a conditional order (only if Suspected complications such as esophagitis, stricture, or poor response to acid suppression)

demographics: Most infants stop spitting up by 12–14 months

risk_factors.text: Neurologic impairment such as cerebral palsy

chief_complaints.text: My baby spits up all the time
She cries and arches her back after feeding

hpi.onset: Begins in the first weeks to months of life, often by age 2–4 months
hpi.duration: Spitting up may continue for months; most improve by 6–12 months and resolve by 12–18 months
hpi.progression: Frequent effortless regurgitation after feeds; tends to peak around 2–4 months and then gradually improve as the lower esophageal sphincter matures
hpi.location: Chest and throat; regurgitated milk comes up from the stomach
hpi.quality: Effortless, non-projectile regurgitation; infant is otherwise comfortable unless esophagitis develops
hpi.severity: Mild; mostly a concern because of volume and frequency, not pain
hpi.timing: During or shortly after feeding, especially with lying flat, burping, or active movement
aggravating: Jostling or active play after feeding

associated_symptoms.text: Poor feeding or refusing to eat

pertinent_negatives: Eczema or blood in stool suggesting milk protein allergy

atypical.how_it_differs: Preterm infants and those with neurologic impairment may have more severe reflux, with apnea, bradycardia, or poor weight gain rather than simple spitting up.
Reflux persisting after 18 months is unusual and should prompt evaluation for other causes, such as anatomic obstruction or eosinophilic esophagitis.

general.mild: Well-appearing, active infant with normal growth and no respiratory distress
general.moderate: Well-appearing but may be fussy during or after feeds; occasional coughing or gagging without respiratory distress
general.severe: Irritable, may have poor weight gain; possibly coughing or wheezing but usually no acute respiratory distress
general.critical: Lethargic, pale, or apneic if severe complications such as aspiration or apnea occur (rare)

findings.maneuver: Observe the infant during and shortly after a feeding, especially when burping or lying supine
findings.finding: Effortless regurgitation of milk or formula

findings.maneuver: Observe the infant during and after feeding
findings.finding: Crying or fussiness, especially with feeds

findings.maneuver: Measure weight, length, and head circumference and plot on growth charts
findings.finding: Growth parameters within normal limits for age

findings.maneuver: Measure weight, length, and head circumference and plot on growth charts
findings.finding: Weight or length for age below expected or crossing downward percentiles

findings.maneuver: Palpate the epigastrium for an olive-shaped mass

findings.finding: Clear breath sounds, no wheezes or crackles

findings.maneuver: Assess skin turgor, mucous membranes, and anterior fontanelle
findings.finding: Moist mucous membranes, normal skin turgor, flat anterior fontanelle
Alert and responsive with normal tone

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected anatomic obstruction such as malrotation, pyloric stenosis, or hiatal hernia

findings.text: Gastroesophageal reflux of barium into the distal esophagus
Normal esophageal and gastric anatomy without obstruction

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected esophagitis, stricture, or eosinophilic esophagitis

findings.text: Erythema or erosions in the distal esophagus

imaging.preferred_when: Projectile vomiting or suspected pyloric stenosis

initial.why: Evaluates for anatomic causes such as malrotation, pyloric stenosis, or hiatal hernia when alarm symptoms are present
initial.only_if: Projectile or bilious vomiting, poor weight gain, or suspected anatomic obstruction
Projectile vomiting or suspected pyloric stenosis

confirmatory.why: Measures acid and non-acid reflux events; confirms GERD when diagnosis is unclear or symptoms are refractory
confirmatory.only_if: Diagnosis uncertain after clinical evaluation and trial of feeding modifications, or suspected refractory GERD

confirmatory.why: Evaluates for esophagitis, stricture, or eosinophilic esophagitis
confirmatory.only_if: Suspected complications such as esophagitis, stricture, or poor response to acid suppression

not_indicated.why: No role unless dehydration or electrolyte disturbance is suspected
Not useful for reflux; only if bowel obstruction suspected

decision_points: Start with feeding modifications and upright positioning before any testing
Evaluate for anatomic obstruction if projectile or bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, or poor weight gain
Consider pH/impedance monitoring or endoscopy if symptoms persist despite nonpharmacologic measures or are severe

criteria.name: Rome IV criteria for infant regurgitation
criteria.summary: Paraphrased: otherwise healthy infant aged 3 weeks to 12 months with regurgitation at least twice daily for 3 or more weeks, without retching, hematemesis, aspiration, apnea, failure to thrive, feeding or swallowing difficulties, or abnormal posturing.
items: Regurgitation 2 or more times per day for 3 or more weeks
No retching, hematemesis, aspiration, apnea, failure to thrive, feeding or swallowing difficulties, or abnormal posturing

differential.name: Pyloric stenosis
differential.why_considered: Projectile vomiting in an infant, especially age 2 to 8 weeks

history: Projectile vomiting shortly after every feed
Hungry after vomiting and willing to feed again
exam: Palpable olive-shaped mass in the epigastrium
imaging: Thickened and elongated pylorus on ultrasound

differential.name: Malrotation with midgut volvulus
differential.why_considered: Bilious vomiting and abdominal distension in an infant

imaging: Upper GI series showing abnormal duodenal-jejunal junction or corkscrew appearance

differential.name: Cow milk protein allergy
differential.why_considered: Irritability, regurgitation, and poor weight gain in a formula-fed infant

history: Symptoms improve after switching to hydrolyzed formula

differential.name: Viral gastroenteritis
differential.why_considered: Vomiting and irritability in an infant

history: Sick contacts or recent viral illness
exam: Diffuse mild abdominal tenderness or no tenderness

differential.name: Eosinophilic esophagitis
differential.why_considered: Persistent reflux-like symptoms despite feeding changes and acid suppression

imaging: Upper endoscopy with biopsy showing eosinophilic infiltration

severity.mild: Uncomplicated physiologic reflux: effortless regurgitation after feeds, normal growth and development, no distress
severity.moderate: Symptomatic reflux with irritability, occasional cough or gagging, normal growth but requiring feeding modifications
severity.severe: Complicated GERD: poor weight gain or feeding refusal, suspected esophagitis, persistent symptoms despite nonpharmacologic measures

red_flags.meaning: Suggests pyloric stenosis or other gastric outlet obstruction; needs abdominal ultrasound
Malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise; surgical emergency

red_flags.finding: Poor weight gain or crossing down percentiles
red_flags.meaning: Complicated GERD, anatomic obstruction, or intolerance; needs further workup
Reflux-associated apnea, aspiration, or other serious disorder; needs urgent evaluation
Esophagitis, gastritis, or other GI bleeding
Bowel obstruction or other abdominal pathology
Infection such as gastroenteritis, sepsis, or urinary tract infection
Dehydration, sepsis, or metabolic abnormality; needs urgent evaluation

complications.name: Failure to thrive / poor weight gain
Esophagitis
clues: Irritability or back arching after feeding

complications.name: Aspiration pneumonia
clues: Cough, wheezing, or respiratory distress after feeds

special_populations.differences: Reflux persisting after 18 months is unusual and should prompt evaluation for eosinophilic esophagitis, anatomic obstruction, or neurologic disorders.
Preterm and neurologically impaired infants may present with apnea, bradycardia, or poor weight gain rather than simple spitting up.

key_questions.question: How old is your baby, and when did the spitting up start?
key_questions.looking_for: Age between 3 weeks and 12 months; onset in first weeks to months, not present at birth or after 12 months

key_questions.question: Can you describe how the spit-up happens? Is it forceful and shoots out, or does it just dribble out with a burp?
How often does your baby spit up, and how much comes up each time?
key_questions.looking_for: Frequent small amounts after feeds; large volume or forceful suggests other causes

key_questions.question: Does your baby seem uncomfortable, cry, or arch their back during or after feeds?
key_questions.looking_for: Irritability or back arching suggests esophagitis; simple reflux is usually painless

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any trouble breathing, turning blue, or unusual limpness during or after feeds?
key_questions.looking_for: Absence of apnea, cyanosis, or limpness; presence suggests complicated GERD or other condition

key_questions.question: Is your baby growing well and gaining weight?
key_questions.looking_for: Normal weight gain; poor weight gain suggests complicated GERD, anatomic obstruction, or allergy

key_questions.question: What color is the spit-up? Is it ever green (bile) or bloody?
key_questions.looking_for: Non-bilious, non-bloody; bilious suggests malrotation; bloody suggests esophagitis or other bleeding

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any fever, diarrhea, or decreased urine output?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests infection, gastroenteritis, or dehydration

key_questions.question: What does your baby eat, and how much? Have you changed formulas or added cereal?
key_questions.looking_for: Overfeeding, rapid feeding, or formula type can worsen reflux; thickening may help

key_questions.question: Does your baby have any medical conditions, or were they born early?
key_questions.looking_for: Prematurity, neurologic impairment, previous esophageal surgery, or hiatal hernia increase risk

key_questions.question: Does your baby have any skin rashes, eczema, or blood/mucus in the stool?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; presence suggests cow milk protein allergy

key_questions.question: Have you tried anything like keeping upright after feeds or burping more? Did it help?
key_questions.looking_for: Response to non-pharmacologic measures supports diagnosis; no or partial response may need further evaluation

reasoning_points: Infant between 3 weeks and 12 months with effortless regurgitation after feeds
Normal growth and development, no weight loss
No projectile, bilious, or bloody vomiting
Meets clinical criteria for typical infant regurgitation (age, frequency, absence of warning signs)
Feeding history reveals overfeeding or air swallowing; response to upright positioning and smaller feeds supports diagnosis
Differential considerations excluded: pyloric stenosis, malrotation, cow milk protein allergy, infection
Diagnosis is clinical; no testing indicated unless alarm features are present

easy: Healthy 2-month-old infant with effortless regurgitation after feeds
No alarm signs; mother reports spitting up several times a day but otherwise thriving
medium: Formula-fed infant with irritability and crying after feeds, prompting concern for cow milk protein allergy
Infant with recurrent cough or gagging during feeds but normal growth, requiring differentiation from aspiration or anatomic issues
Infant whose symptoms improve only partially with feeding modifications, leading to consideration of acid suppression trial
hard: Infant with projectile non-bilious vomiting and dehydration, requiring urgent evaluation for pyloric stenosis
Infant with bilious vomiting and abdominal distension, needing immediate workup for malrotation with volvulus
Preterm infant with apnea, bradycardia, and desaturations during feeds, requiring investigation for reflux-related apnea and GERD
Infant with persistent irritability, poor weight gain, and suspected esophagitis or eosinophilic esophagitis despite standard management
